_comment: One index card per Component 4 topic, keyed by spec number. `blurb` says what the topic is; `teaches` is what a student will be able to do. Written from each topic's own Curriculum-Topics spec file and its curated subtopic list. UK English. `destination` is where the card sends a student: a topic hub here, a bench that is already public, or an honest members door when no free page exists. Nothing here is generated — edit this file and re-run scripts/compile-map-room-graph.py.

1.1.blurb: The studio as one system — how the computer, the interface and your controllers hand audio to each other, and what each setting costs you
teaches: What the DAW does that a plug-in cannot
How an interface turns sound into data
Why buffer size trades latency against stability
Which connector each job actually needs

1.2.blurb: Everything a recording will ever contain arrives through the microphone — where you put it decides more than any plug-in can undo later
teaches: Choosing a microphone type for the source
Reading polar patterns and off-axis colour
Setting gain before anything else
Why two microphones can cancel each other

1.3.blurb: Sound built from nothing — an oscillator makes the raw tone, then filters and envelopes shape it into something playable
teaches: What each waveform's harmonics sound like
How filters remove and emphasise frequencies
How an envelope gives a sound its shape
Using an LFO to put movement in

1.4.blurb: Recorded sound as raw material — crop it, stretch it, reverse it, and it becomes an instrument you never played
teaches: Cropping a breakbeat down to a usable loop
Changing pitch without changing tempo
Warping a sample to the project tempo
What clearance a released track needs

1.5.blurb: MIDI carries instructions, not sound — which is why a sequenced part can be re-timed, re-voiced and corrected long after you played it
teaches: Recording in real time or step by step
What quantise fixes and what it flattens
Editing velocity and note length for feel
How pitch bend and tempo data travel

1.6.blurb: Where one good take gets assembled out of several imperfect ones — quietly enough that nobody hears the joins
teaches: Comping a lead from multiple takes
Cutting at zero crossings to avoid clicks
Using fades to hide an edit
Staying non-destructive until the bounce

1.7.blurb: Correction is a judgement, not a button — how far you pull a performance toward the grid changes what it sounds like
teaches: Tuning without losing the singer's formants
Choosing a warp mode to suit the material
Quantising rhythm while keeping the groove
Working offline against working in real time

1.8.blurb: Automation is the mix moving — a level, a filter or a send that changes over time so the arrangement keeps developing
teaches: Writing volume and pan moves over time
Automating an effect rather than a level
Choosing curve shapes for smooth changes
Editing breakpoints and clip envelopes

1.9.blurb: These processors act on level alone — holding loud moments back and lifting quiet ones, which is what makes a mix breathe
teaches: Setting threshold and ratio for the source
How attack and release shape a transient
Gating, expansion and de-essing in practice
Reading a compression or gating graph

1.10.blurb: Two speakers, one image — stereo is built from timing and level differences that your ears read as direction and width
teaches: Choosing a stereo microphone pair for the room
Panning to place a sound, not just to spread it
Why width can collapse when summed to mono
Using the Haas effect deliberately

1.11.blurb: EQ is subtraction as often as addition — you make room for one sound by taking frequencies out of another
teaches: Shelves, bands and high-pass filters
What Q actually changes
Sweeping to find a problem frequency
Clearing sibilance, hum and rumble

1.12d.blurb: A repeat you can place in time — long enough to hear as an echo, short enough to stop being one and become a tone
teaches: Syncing repeats to the project tempo
What feedback adds, and when it runs away
Slapback, ping-pong and multi-tap in use
Why very short delays comb-filter

1.12m.blurb: A parameter moving on its own — one LFO sits behind chorus, flanging, phasing and tremolo alike
teaches: How rate, depth and waveform change the effect
What separates chorus, flanger and phaser
Tremolo against vibrato — level or pitch
Ring modulation's carrier and modulator

1.12r.blurb: The room you did not record in — its size, its surfaces, and how long it takes for the sound to disappear
teaches: Pre-delay, decay and damping in practice
Algorithmic against convolution reverb
Sending to a reverb rather than inserting it
Gated and reverse reverb as effects

1.12x.blurb: Controlled damage — clipping a waveform adds harmonics that were never in the original sound
teaches: Overdrive, fuzz, saturation and bitcrushing
Hard clipping against soft clipping
Why symmetry decides which harmonics appear
Keeping gain staging under control

1.13.blurb: The mix before the effects — faders, panning and space arranged so every part can be heard without fighting
teaches: Building a static mix first
Finding and clearing frequency masking
Creating depth with reverb and delay
Checking in mono and on other speakers

1.14.blurb: The last pass — making a finished mix sit alongside commercial releases without crushing what the mix was doing
teaches: Loudness targets and true peak limits
What glue and multiband compression do
Mid-side moves and keeping bass mono
Preparing files for each delivery format

2.1.blurb: The room is part of the signal chain — its reflections arrive with every recording whether you wanted them or not
teaches: What RT60 measures
Direct sound against reverberant sound
Where room modes build up
Absorption or diffusion, and when

2.2.blurb: You can only mix what you hear — a monitor's job is to tell you the truth, including the parts you would rather not know
teaches: How drivers and crossovers split the band
Why flat response beats a flattering one
Placing monitors and taming boundaries
What headphones and small speakers hide

2.3.blurb: How audio survives the journey down a cable — and why the wrong connection adds noise no EQ will take back out
teaches: Balanced against unbalanced connections
Reading TRS, TS and XLR wiring
What common-mode rejection removes
When a DI box is the right answer

2.4.blurb: Turning a continuous wave into numbers and back again — every conversion sets a limit on what can be recorded
teaches: What sample rate and bit depth each decide
Why Nyquist sets the ceiling
How aliasing appears, and how to avoid it
What analogue still does differently

2.5.blurb: The working-out the exam asks for — delay times, dynamic range, gain changes, each one answering a practical studio question
teaches: Working out delay times from tempo
Moving between octaves, semitones and cents
Reading the decibel scale and its ratios
Checking a sample rate against Nyquist

2.6.blurb: Level is the one thing every stage shares — set it wrong early and no amount of later processing fully recovers it
teaches: dBu, dBV and dBFS, and where each applies
Peak, RMS, VU and LUFS metering
Gain staging through the whole chain
Staying clear of clipping and the noise floor
